title: A Morning Prayer in Flight
superscription: A Psalm of David, when he fled from his son Absalom.

verses.text: O LORD, how my foes have increased! How many rise up against me!
Many say of me, "God will not deliver him." Selah
But You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head.
To the LORD I cry aloud, and He answers me from His holy mountain. Selah
I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me.
I will not fear the myriads set against me on every side.
Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! Strike all my enemies on the jaw; break the teeth of the wicked.
Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people. Selah

context.author: The title says “of David” (Hebrew le-David), which can mean by David, for David or about David. Seventy-three psalms carry his name; tradition and the New Testament take many of them as his.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.mapLabel: DAVID FLEEING FROM ABSALOM, ACROSS THE JORDAN
context.setting: The title sets the scene: “A Psalm of David, when he fled from his son Absalom.” Absalom had seized the throne, and David left Jerusalem weeping, crossed the Jordan and went to Mahanaim (2 Samuel 15-17). “O LORD, how my foes have increased!” he prays, as many say, “God will not deliver him” (vv.1-2). “But You, O LORD, are a shield around me” (v.3). He sleeps and wakes, because the LORD sustains him (v.5), and will not fear “the myriads set against me on every side” (v.6). “Salvation belongs to the LORD” (v.8).
context.custom: Selah (vv.2, 4, 8) appears 71 times in the Psalms; its meaning is uncertain. It may mark a pause, a musical interlude or a change of voice. Lifting someone’s head (v.3) meant restoring honor, as a king lifted the head of a pardoned servant (Genesis 40:13). Striking an enemy on the jaw (v.7) was a public insult.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 4 is an evening prayer: “I will lie down and sleep in peace.”
context.timelineBible: 2 Samuel 15:13-17:24 tells how David fled from Absalom barefoot and weeping up the Mount of Olives, and crossed the Jordan to Mahanaim, where friends brought him food. Absalom was killed in battle in the forest of Ephraim (2 Samuel 18).

overview.discussion: David slept in the middle of a crisis (v.5). What keeps me awake, and what would it mean to rest in God tonight?
